subject: Biology
q: Who first used the word “cell”, after observing thin slices of cork under a simple microscope in 1665?
explanation: Robert Hooke saw tiny box-like compartments in cork (actually the walls of dead cells) and called them “cells”, like small rooms. Leeuwenhoek later saw living cells; Brown discovered the nucleus (1831); Schleiden and Schwann proposed cell theory (1838–39).
hints: He described what he saw in his book “Micrographia”.

subject: Biology
q: Lysosomes are sometimes called the “suicide bags” of the cell. Why?
options: They make the cell divide uncontrollably.
They produce poisons that kill other cells.
They contain powerful digestive enzymes that can break down the cell itself if they burst.
They store all the cell’s water.
explanation: Lysosomes are membrane-bound sacs of digestive enzymes that break down worn-out organelles and engulfed material. When a cell is badly damaged, lysosomes may burst and digest the cell — hence the nickname.
hints: What do lysosomes contain?

subject: Biology
q: Cells of the pancreas that secrete large amounts of digestive enzymes have an especially well-developed Golgi apparatus. Why?
options: The Golgi apparatus modifies, packages and dispatches proteins for secretion.
The Golgi apparatus releases energy from food.
explanation: Proteins made on the rough ER are sent to the Golgi apparatus, which modifies them and packs them into vesicles that carry them to the cell membrane for release. Secretory cells therefore have a large Golgi apparatus (and plenty of rough ER).
misconception: Energy release is the job of mitochondria.
hints: Which organelle acts as the cell’s “packaging and dispatch centre”?

subject: Biology
q: Red blood cells are placed in pure distilled water, while plant leaf cells are placed in the same water. What happens?
options: The plant cells burst; the red blood cells shrink.
The red blood cells swell and burst; the plant cells swell but do not burst because of their cell walls.
explanation: Pure water has a higher water concentration than cell contents, so water enters both by osmosis. Animal cells have only a thin membrane and burst (haemolysis). Plant cells swell until their rigid cellulose wall pushes back (turgor), preventing bursting — which is how turgid cells keep leaves firm.
hints: Which way does water move by osmosis in each case?
What structure do plant cells have that animal cells lack?

subject: Biology
q: How does rough endoplasmic reticulum differ from smooth endoplasmic reticulum?
options: Rough ER has ribosomes on its surface and makes proteins; smooth ER makes lipids and helps detoxify drugs and poisons.
Rough ER is found only in plants.
Rough ER stores starch; smooth ER makes DNA.
Smooth ER has ribosomes; rough ER does not.
explanation: The ER is a network of membranes. Ribosomes attached to rough ER give it a “rough” look and synthesise proteins. Smooth ER lacks ribosomes and makes lipids such as membrane phospholipids and steroid hormones; in liver cells it detoxifies many poisons.
hints: What gives rough ER its rough appearance?

subject: Biology
q: Under a microscope magnifying 500 times, the image of a cell measures 5 mm across. What is the real size of the cell? (1 mm = 1000 μm)
explanation: Real size = image size ÷ magnification = 5 mm ÷ 500 = 0.01 mm = 10 μm — typical of many animal cells.
misconception: 2.5 mm multiplies instead of dividing.
hints: Actual size = image size ÷ magnification.
Convert mm to μm by multiplying by 1000.

subject: Biology
q: How does oxygen enter a cell from the surrounding fluid?
options: Only by active transport using energy
By diffusion, from higher to lower oxygen concentration, through the membrane
explanation: Small molecules such as O₂ and CO₂ diffuse through the membrane down their concentration gradient. Cells use oxygen continuously, keeping its concentration inside lower. Osmosis refers specifically to the movement of WATER through a selectively permeable membrane.
misconception: Osmosis is only for water, not for gases.
hints: Osmosis is the special case of which molecule?

subject: Biology
q: Chromosomes, which carry the genes, are found mainly in which part of a eukaryotic cell?
explanation: Chromosomes are long DNA molecules wrapped around proteins, housed in the nucleus. They become visible as compact structures when a cell divides. (Mitochondria and chloroplasts also carry a little DNA of their own.)
hints: Which organelle is the cell’s control centre?

subject: Biology
q: Consider two cube-shaped cells: one 1 μm on each side and one 10 μm on each side. What is the surface-area-to-volume ratio of the SMALLER cell (in μm⁻¹), and why does this matter?
options: 0.06 — small cells cannot exchange enough materials
6 — a high ratio lets substances diffuse in and out fast enough to supply the whole cell
0.6 — small cells receive less oxygen per volume
60 — a ratio that makes small cells burst
explanation: Small cube: area 6 × 1² = 6 μm², volume 1 μm³, ratio 6. Large cube: area 600 μm², volume 1000 μm³, ratio 0.6. As a cell grows, its volume (needs) rises faster than its surface (supply route), so diffusion becomes too slow. This is a key reason cells stay small and large organisms are multicellular.
misconception: 0.6 is the ratio for the LARGER cell.
hints: Area of a cube = 6s²; volume = s³.
Which grows faster as s increases: area or volume?

subject: Biology
q: The red colour of a ripe tomato and the storage of starch in potato tubers are due to two kinds of plastids. Which?
explanation: Plastids are plant organelles. Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll; chromoplasts contain other pigments (red, orange, yellow) in fruits and flowers; leucoplasts are colourless and store starch, oils or proteins.
hints: “Chromo” means colour; “leuco” means white.

subject: Biology
q: Stomata are small pores in the epidermis of leaves. What controls their opening and closing?
options: A pair of guard cells around each pore
explanation: Each stoma is surrounded by two kidney-shaped guard cells. When they take in water and become turgid they curve apart, opening the pore; when they lose water they close it — controlling gas exchange and water loss.
hints: The cells around the pore change shape.

subject: Biology
q: The leaf stalks and young stems of many plants bend in the wind without breaking. Which tissue provides this flexibility?
explanation: Collenchyma cells are living, elongated and thickened at their corners, giving mechanical support with flexibility. Sclerenchyma is rigid (dead, lignified cells), giving strength but not bendiness.
hints: Which supporting tissue is living and thickened only at the corners?

subject: Biology
q: The hard husk of a coconut and the strings in jute are made of sclerenchyma. What feature of these cells gives such strength?
options: Thick walls deposited with lignin; the cells are dead when mature
explanation: Sclerenchyma cells have very thick walls impregnated with lignin, a tough polymer, and often no living contents at maturity. They give hardness and tensile strength (fibres used in jute and coir ropes).
hints: Which substance makes wood hard?

subject: Biology
q: The walls of lung alveoli and blood capillaries are lined by a single layer of very thin, flat cells. Why?
options: It stops all substances passing through.
A thin squamous epithelium gives the shortest distance for rapid diffusion of gases and nutrients.
explanation: Simple squamous epithelium is just one flattened cell thick, so oxygen, carbon dioxide and nutrients have very little distance to diffuse. Skin, which must resist wear, has many layers (stratified epithelium) instead.
hints: What process happens across these walls?

subject: Biology
q: In a neuron, which part carries the nerve impulse AWAY from the cell body towards the next cell?
options: The cell membrane of the cell body only
explanation: Dendrites receive signals and carry them towards the cell body; the long axon conducts the impulse away to its terminals, which pass it to another neuron, muscle or gland. Some axons in the human body are about a metre long.
misconception: Dendrites carry impulses towards the cell body, not away.
hints: Which part is the long “cable” of a neuron?

subject: Biology
q: Your ear and the tip of your nose can be bent but spring back, whereas the bones of your arm cannot bend. What is the key difference between these tissues?
options: Cartilage has a flexible protein matrix; bone’s matrix is hardened with calcium and phosphate minerals.
Bone is not a living tissue.
Cartilage is a type of muscle.
explanation: Both are connective tissues with cells in a matrix. Cartilage’s matrix is rich in flexible proteins and polysaccharides, so it is firm but bendable. Bone’s matrix is mineralised with calcium phosphate, making it hard and rigid. Bone also has blood vessels; cartilage has very few.
misconception: Bone is living tissue — it grows, repairs fractures and makes blood cells in its marrow.
hints: Both are connective tissues — what is in their matrix?
Which mineral makes bones hard?

subject: Biology
q: Which connective tissue stores fat below the skin and helps insulate the body?
explanation: Adipose tissue is made of cells filled with fat droplets. It stores energy, cushions organs and reduces heat loss. Whales and seals rely on thick adipose layers (blubber).
hints: “Adipose” means fatty.

subject: Biology
q: Phloem sieve tubes have no nucleus when mature but are accompanied by companion cells. Why are companion cells important?
options: They carry out the metabolic work (and supply energy) that keeps the sieve tubes functioning.
They store water for the xylem.
explanation: Mature sieve-tube elements lose their nucleus and most organelles, leaving an open channel for transporting sugars. Each is linked to a companion cell with a nucleus and many mitochondria, which supplies proteins and energy needed for loading and transporting food.
hints: What has a sieve tube lost that a living cell normally needs?

subject: Biology
q: The bark of old trees contains cork cells. What is true of them?
options: They are dead, tightly packed and coated with suberin, which makes them waterproof.
They carry water up the tree.
explanation: Cork cells are dead at maturity and have walls impregnated with suberin, a waxy substance. The layer protects the tree against water loss, infection and injury. Bottle corks are made from the bark of the cork oak.
hints: Bottle corks come from this tissue.

subject: Biology
q: The lining of your windpipe (trachea) is covered with ciliated epithelium and mucus-secreting cells. How does this protect the lungs?
options: Mucus traps dust and microbes, and beating cilia sweep it upward to the throat to be swallowed or coughed out.
Cilia pump air into the lungs.
explanation: The coordinated beating of cilia moves the mucus “escalator” away from the lungs. Smoking paralyses and damages cilia, so mucus builds up — one cause of “smoker’s cough” and frequent chest infections.
hints: What do sticky mucus and moving hairs do together?

subject: Biology
q: Which kingdom contains organisms whose cells have no membrane-bound nucleus?
explanation: Monera are prokaryotes — bacteria and cyanobacteria (blue-green algae). Their DNA lies free in the cytoplasm. All the other four kingdoms are eukaryotes.
hints: Which kingdom contains bacteria?

subject: Biology
q: Amoeba, Paramecium and Euglena belong to which kingdom?
explanation: They are unicellular eukaryotes (they have a nucleus), so they belong to Protista. Amoeba moves by pseudopodia, Paramecium by cilia and Euglena by a flagellum.
misconception: Being single-celled does not make them Monera — they have a true nucleus.
hints: They are single-celled but have a nucleus.

subject: Biology
q: Mosses and liverworts (bryophytes) are called the “amphibians of the plant kingdom”. Why?
options: They live on land but need water for their male gametes to swim to the eggs.
They can breathe both in water and on land.
They change from fish-like to frog-like forms.
explanation: Bryophytes have no true vascular tissue and their sperm must swim through a film of water to fertilise eggs. So, like amphibians, they live on land but depend on water to reproduce, and they grow in damp, shady places.
hints: How do their sperm reach the eggs?

subject: Biology
q: Ferns have roots, stems, leaves and vascular tissue, but they belong to a different group from flowering plants. What is the key difference?
options: Ferns reproduce by spores and do not produce seeds.
Ferns have no xylem or phloem.
explanation: Ferns are pteridophytes: vascular plants that reproduce by spores (seen as brown dots under the leaves). Gymnosperms and angiosperms produce seeds. Bryophytes have neither true vascular tissue nor seeds.
hints: Look under a fern leaf. What are the brown dots?

subject: Biology
q: Euglena has chloroplasts and can photosynthesise, but it can also swim using a flagellum and absorb food in the dark. Why is it classified in Protista rather than as a plant or an animal?
options: It is a single-celled eukaryote with features of both plants and animals, which fits the broad kingdom of unicellular eukaryotes.
It is a type of bacterium.
explanation: Euglena shows why the old two-kingdom (plant/animal) system failed. It photosynthesises like a plant but moves and can feed heterotrophically like an animal. Whittaker’s five-kingdom system placed such unicellular eukaryotes together in Protista.
hints: Does Euglena fit neatly into “plant” or “animal”?
What kingdom groups single-celled organisms with a nucleus?

subject: Biology
q: Insects, spiders, crabs and centipedes belong to the largest animal phylum. Which feature do they share?
options: Jointed legs and a hard exoskeleton
explanation: Arthropoda (“jointed feet”) have jointed appendages, a segmented body and a chitinous exoskeleton. Over three-quarters of all known animal species are arthropods, most of them insects.
hints: “Arthro” means joint and “poda” means feet.

subject: Biology
q: Which pairing of an animal with its phylum is correct?
explanation: Hydra and jellyfish are cnidarians with stinging cells and a single body opening. Tapeworms are flatworms (Platyhelminthes); earthworms are segmented worms (Annelida); starfish are Echinodermata.
hints: Which phylum has stinging cells and tentacles?

subject: Biology
q:
Consider:
I. Birds and mammals are warm-blooded.
II. All reptiles and amphibians are warm-blooded.
III. All mammals give birth to live young.
IV. All birds lay eggs.
Which are correct?
explanation: Only birds and mammals maintain a constant body temperature (I true; II false). A few mammals, the monotremes such as the platypus and echidna, lay eggs (III false). All birds lay eggs (IV true).
hints: Think of the platypus.

subject: Biology
q: Which set of features best describes amphibians such as frogs?
options: Moist skin that helps in breathing, eggs laid in water, and a larval stage (tadpole) that changes form
Dry scaly skin and eggs with shells laid on land
explanation: Amphibians have moist, permeable skin used partly for gas exchange, lay jelly-coated eggs in water, and undergo metamorphosis from gilled tadpoles to air-breathing adults. Reptiles have dry scales and shelled eggs.
hints: Think of the frog’s life cycle.

subject: Biology
q: A whale lives in the sea and has a streamlined, fish-like shape. Which evidence shows it is a mammal and not a fish?
options: It breathes air with lungs, is warm-blooded and feeds its young on milk.
explanation: Whales must surface to breathe through blowholes, maintain a constant body temperature, have a few hairs (especially as calves) and suckle their young with milk. Their fish-like shape is convergent evolution — similar solutions to the same environment.
misconception: Shape and habitat are not reliable bases for classification.
hints: How does a whale breathe?
How does a whale feed its young?

subject: Biology
q: Which order correctly lists the levels of classification from the broadest to the most specific?
options: Kingdom → Class → Phylum → Family → Order → Genus → Species
Phylum → Kingdom → Order → Class → Genus → Family → Species
Species → Genus → Family → Order → Class → Phylum → Kingdom
Kingdom → Phylum → Class → Order → Family → Genus → Species
explanation: Each level contains one or more groups from the level below. A kingdom contains many phyla; a genus contains closely related species. (A memory aid: “King Philip Came Over For Good Soup”.)
hints: Species is the most specific level.

subject: Biology
q: A plant has leaves with parallel veins, a fibrous root system, and flower parts in multiples of three. Its seed has one cotyledon. Which plant could it be?
explanation: All these features — one cotyledon, parallel venation, fibrous roots, flower parts in threes — are typical of monocotyledons such as maize, wheat, rice and grasses. Dicots like pea and mango have two cotyledons, net venation and a taproot.
hints: How many cotyledons does it have?

subject: Biology
q: Which is the largest gland in the human body?
explanation: The liver (about 1.5 kg in adults) produces bile, stores glycogen, detoxifies substances and makes many blood proteins. The pituitary, though tiny, is called the master gland because it controls other endocrine glands.
hints: It produces bile.

subject: Biology
q: Which gland–hormone pairing is correct?
explanation: The pituitary secretes growth hormone (and hormones controlling other glands). The thyroid makes thyroxine; the pancreas makes insulin (and glucagon); the adrenal glands make adrenaline; the ovaries make oestrogen.
hints: Which gland is called the master gland?

subject: Biology
q: Just before a big race, an athlete’s heart pounds and breathing speeds up. Which hormone is mainly responsible, and why is the response useful?
options: Adrenaline — it delivers more oxygen and glucose to muscles in preparation for action
explanation: Adrenaline from the adrenal glands prepares the body for “fight or flight”: it increases heart rate and breathing, diverts blood to muscles and raises blood glucose, so muscles can work hard immediately.
hints: Which hormone is released in fear or excitement?

subject: Biology
q: Nerve impulses always travel in one direction across a synapse (the gap between two neurons). Why?
options: Gravity pulls the impulse one way.
Chemical messengers (neurotransmitters) are released only from the axon ending and detected only by receptors on the next cell.
The gap is too wide for electricity in the other direction.
explanation: At a synapse, the electrical impulse causes the axon terminal to release neurotransmitter molecules. These diffuse across the gap and bind to receptors on the next neuron’s dendrite, starting a new impulse. Only the axon end stores neurotransmitter and only the receiving side has receptors, so transmission is one-way.
hints: What crosses the synaptic gap — electricity or chemicals?
Which side releases them and which side detects them?

subject: Biology
q: A person whose kidneys have failed is treated with dialysis. What does the dialysis machine do?
options: Removes urea and excess salts and water from the blood by passing it along a selectively permeable membrane
Pumps blood in place of the heart
explanation: In haemodialysis, blood flows past a selectively permeable membrane bathed in dialysis fluid. Small waste molecules such as urea diffuse out into the fluid, while blood cells and proteins stay in the blood — doing the kidney’s filtering job.
hints: Which waste product do kidneys mainly remove?

subject: Biology
q: The kidneys filter about 180 litres of fluid from the blood each day, yet only about 1.5 litres of urine is produced. What percentage of the filtered fluid is reabsorbed?
explanation: Reabsorbed = 180 − 1.5 = 178.5 L; 178.5/180 × 100 ≈ 99.2%. Nephron tubules reabsorb nearly all the water, glucose and useful salts, leaving a small volume of concentrated waste.
misconception: 0.8% is the fraction that is NOT reabsorbed (excreted).
hints: How much of the 180 L is not lost as urine?
Divide the reabsorbed volume by the filtered volume.

subject: Biology
q: Why does a doctor not prescribe antibiotics for a common cold?
options: Antibiotics are too strong for colds.
Colds are caused by viruses, and antibiotics act on bacterial structures that viruses do not have.
explanation: Antibiotics such as penicillin work by attacking bacterial cell walls, ribosomes or enzymes. Viruses lack these and reproduce inside our own cells, so antibiotics have no effect on them. Unnecessary use also helps bacteria evolve resistance.
hints: What kind of microbe causes the common cold?

subject: Biology
q: In the ABO blood group system, why can a person with blood group O usually donate red cells to people of any ABO group?
options: Group O blood has no plasma.
Group O red cells carry neither A nor B antigens, so the recipient’s antibodies have nothing to attack.
Group O blood contains no red cells.
Group O blood contains both A and B antigens.
explanation: A recipient’s plasma contains antibodies against the antigens their own cells lack (e.g. group A has anti-B). Donated red cells clump if they carry an antigen the recipient has antibodies against. Group O cells have no A or B antigens, so they are not attacked — the “universal donor” (Rh factor must also be matched).
misconception: It is the absence of antigens on the RED CELLS that matters.
hints: What do antibodies in the recipient’s plasma react with?
Which antigens are on group O red cells?

subject: Biology
q: Which of these is NOT a function of the human skeleton?
options: Protecting organs such as the brain and heart
Making blood cells in the bone marrow
explanation: The skeleton supports the body, protects organs (skull, ribcage), allows movement with muscles, stores calcium and makes blood cells in red bone marrow. Digestion is done by the digestive system.
hints: Which option belongs to a different organ system?

subject: Biology
q: Look at a friend’s eyes in dim light, then shine a torch near them. The pupils get smaller. Which part of the eye causes this, and why?
options: The iris contracts around the pupil to reduce the light entering and protect the retina.
The lens shrinks to block light.
explanation: The iris is a ring of muscle that controls the size of the pupil reflexively. In bright light it makes the pupil smaller to prevent damage and glare; in dim light it widens the pupil to let in more light.
hints: Which coloured part of the eye surrounds the pupil?

subject: Biology
q: Malaria is caused by which type of organism, and how does it spread?
options: A virus, spread by contaminated water
A protozoan (Plasmodium), spread by the bite of infected female Anopheles mosquitoes
explanation: Plasmodium is a single-celled protozoan that multiplies in the liver and red blood cells. Female Anopheles mosquitoes carry it from person to person when they feed on blood. Nets, repellents and removing stagnant water help prevent it.
hints: Which insect carries malaria?

subject: Biology
q: Which nutrient is the body’s main and quickest source of energy?
explanation: Carbohydrates (starch and sugars from cereals, potatoes and fruit) are broken down into glucose, which cells respire to release energy. Fats store more energy per gram but release it more slowly; vitamins and minerals provide no energy.
hints: Rice, wheat and potatoes are rich in this nutrient.

subject: Biology
q: A child with a swollen belly, thin limbs and stunted growth is diagnosed with kwashiorkor. Which nutrient is deficient?
explanation: Kwashiorkor is caused by severe protein deficiency even when some energy is available. Proteins provide amino acids for growth and for blood proteins that keep fluid in the blood vessels; without them fluid leaks into tissues, causing swelling. Lack of both energy and protein causes marasmus.
hints: Which nutrient is needed for growth and repair?

subject: Biology
q: Why is vitamin D sometimes called the “sunshine vitamin”, and what does its deficiency cause in children?
options: The skin makes it when exposed to sunlight; deficiency causes rickets (soft, bent bones).
It absorbs sunlight; deficiency causes night blindness.
It is found only in sunlight-ripened fruit; deficiency causes scurvy.
It is made by the eyes; deficiency causes goitre.
explanation: Ultraviolet light allows skin to make vitamin D, which is needed to absorb calcium and phosphate for strong bones. Without it, children’s bones stay soft and bend (rickets). Night blindness is vitamin A deficiency; scurvy is vitamin C.
hints: Which mineral’s absorption depends on vitamin D?

subject: Biology
q: Why does a diet poor in iron make a person tired and breathless?
options: Iron is needed to make haemoglobin; with too little, the blood carries less oxygen (anaemia).
Iron is needed for the lungs to expand.
explanation: Each haemoglobin molecule contains four iron atoms that bind oxygen. Too little iron means less haemoglobin and fewer red cells, so tissues get less oxygen — causing fatigue and breathlessness. Green leafy vegetables, jaggery, pulses and meat supply iron.
hints: Which molecule carries oxygen in red blood cells?

subject: Biology
q: Fat provides about 37 kJ per gram and carbohydrate about 17 kJ per gram. How much energy does a snack containing 20 g of fat and 50 g of carbohydrate provide?
explanation: Fat: 20 × 37 = 740 kJ. Carbohydrate: 50 × 17 = 850 kJ. Total = 1590 kJ (about 380 kcal). Fat gives more than twice the energy per gram of carbohydrate.
misconception: 850 kJ counts only the carbohydrate.
hints: Calculate each nutrient’s energy and add.

subject: Biology
q: Dietary fibre (roughage) is not digested by humans. Why is it still important?
options: It is absorbed into the blood as glucose.
It adds bulk to food, helping it move through the intestines and preventing constipation.
It provides most of our energy.
explanation: Fibre, mainly cellulose from plant cell walls, holds water and adds bulk so the intestine muscles can push food along (peristalsis). Whole grains, fruit, vegetables and pulses are good sources.
hints: What helps food move through the gut?

subject: Biology
q: A student tests a food sample. Iodine stays brown, biuret reagent turns violet, and a translucent spot appears when it is rubbed on paper. Which nutrients does the sample contain?
options: Protein and fat, but not starch
Starch and fat, but not protein
explanation: Iodine turns blue-black with starch — no change means no starch. Biuret turns violet with protein. A translucent “grease spot” shows fat. So the sample has protein and fat; it could be, for example, a nut or egg yolk.
hints: Match each test to the nutrient it detects.

subject: Biology
q: Pepsin digests protein in the stomach, where conditions are strongly acidic (pH ≈ 2). If pepsin is placed in a test tube with protein at pH 8, what would you expect?
options: The protein would digest the enzyme.
The same rate, because pH does not affect enzymes.
Faster digestion, because pH 8 is neutral.
Little or no protein digestion, because each enzyme works best at its own optimum pH.
explanation: Enzymes are proteins whose shape depends on pH. Pepsin’s active site works best in acid; at pH 8 its shape changes and it becomes inactive. In the small intestine, where conditions are slightly alkaline, trypsin takes over protein digestion.
misconception: pH 8 is slightly alkaline, not neutral, and “neutral” is not best for every enzyme.
hints: What is the optimum pH of pepsin?
How does pH affect an enzyme’s shape?

subject: Biology
q: In the 19th century, sailors and prisoners who ate mainly polished white rice often developed beriberi (weakness and nerve damage), while those eating unpolished rice did not. Which explanation fits?
options: Polishing removes the husk and bran layers that contain vitamin B1 (thiamine).
Beriberi is caused by a virus in white rice.
explanation: The outer bran layers of rice are rich in thiamine, needed for releasing energy from carbohydrates and for nerve function. Polishing removes them. Studies of this disease (by Eijkman and others) led to the discovery of vitamins.
hints: What is removed when rice is polished?
Which vitamin deficiency causes beriberi?

subject: Biology
q: Which correctly gives the end products of digestion?
options: Starch → fatty acids; proteins → glycerol; fats → glucose
Starch → amino acids; proteins → glucose; fats → starch
Starch → glucose; proteins → amino acids; fats → fatty acids and glycerol
explanation: Digestion breaks large molecules into small soluble ones that can be absorbed through the villi: carbohydrates into simple sugars (glucose), proteins into amino acids, and fats into fatty acids and glycerol.
hints: Proteins are made of which building blocks?

subject: Biology
q: Which teeth are mainly used for grinding and chewing food?
explanation: Incisors (front) cut and bite, canines (pointed) tear, and premolars and molars (broad, ridged) crush and grind. Chewing increases the surface area of food for enzymes.
hints: Which teeth are at the back of the mouth?

subject: Biology
q: What is the difference between breathing and respiration?
options: Breathing happens in cells; respiration happens in the lungs.
Breathing moves air in and out of the lungs; respiration releases energy from food inside cells.
explanation: Breathing (ventilation) is a mechanical process that exchanges air. Cellular respiration is a chemical process in every living cell, especially in mitochondria: glucose is broken down to release energy. Plants respire too, even though they do not “breathe” with lungs.
hints: Which one happens inside every cell?

subject: Biology
q: A student blows through a straw into limewater, which turns milky much faster than when ordinary air is bubbled through it. What does this show?
options: Exhaled air contains more carbon dioxide than inhaled air.
explanation: Limewater (calcium hydroxide solution) turns milky as insoluble calcium carbonate forms with CO₂. Inhaled air has about 0.04% CO₂; exhaled air about 4%, produced by respiration in body cells.
hints: Which gas turns limewater milky?

subject: Biology
q: What happens during inhalation (breathing in)?
options: The diaphragm contracts and flattens and the ribs move up and out, increasing chest volume and lowering pressure, so air flows in.
The lungs pull air in by their own muscles.
The diaphragm relaxes and domes upward, squeezing air in.
explanation: Lungs have no muscles of their own. When the diaphragm and intercostal muscles contract, the chest cavity enlarges, the pressure inside falls below atmospheric pressure, and air rushes in. Relaxation reverses this for exhalation.
misconception: The lungs are passive; the diaphragm and rib muscles do the work.
hints: Air moves from high pressure to low pressure.

subject: Biology
q: At rest, a person breathes 15 times a minute, taking in 0.5 litres of air with each breath. How much air do they breathe per minute?
explanation: Volume per minute = breaths per minute × volume per breath = 15 × 0.5 = 7.5 litres. During hard exercise this can rise more than tenfold.
misconception: 30 L divides 15 by 0.5 instead of multiplying.
hints: Multiply breaths per minute by litres per breath.

subject: Biology
q: Why does bread dough rise when yeast is added and the dough is left in a warm place?
options: Warmth makes flour expand on its own.
Yeast respires anaerobically, producing carbon dioxide bubbles that expand the dough.
explanation: Yeast is a fungus that ferments sugars: glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide + energy. The CO₂ is trapped by the stretchy gluten in the dough, making it rise; the ethanol evaporates during baking. Warmth speeds up the yeast’s enzymes.
hints: Which gas does fermentation release?

subject: Biology
q: Germinating seeds are placed in a sealed flask containing potassium hydroxide solution (which absorbs CO₂). A bent glass tube from the flask dips into a beaker of coloured water. After some hours, the water rises up the tube. What does this show?
options: The seeds took in oxygen during respiration; the CO₂ they released was absorbed, so the gas volume in the flask fell.
explanation: Respiring seeds use O₂ and give out an equal volume of CO₂. The KOH removes the CO₂, so the total volume of gas in the flask decreases and the outside air pressure pushes water up the tube. A control flask with boiled (dead) seeds would show no rise.
misconception: Without KOH, the CO₂ produced would replace the O₂ used and the water level would barely move.
hints: What does KOH remove from the air in the flask?
If oxygen is used up and CO₂ removed, what happens to the gas volume?

subject: Biology
q: Why does a fish suffocate when taken out of water, even though air contains far more oxygen than water?
options: Its delicate gill filaments collapse and stick together in air, leaving too small a surface for gas exchange.
Fish gills only absorb carbon dioxide.
Air is too cold for fish.
Fish cannot use oxygen from air because it is a different gas.
explanation: Gills have many thin filaments and lamellae held apart by water, giving a huge surface area. Out of water they collapse, the surface area shrinks drastically and the gills dry out, so the fish cannot absorb enough oxygen.
hints: What holds the thin gill filaments apart?

subject: Biology
q:
Consider:
I. Plants respire only at night.
II. Plants respire all the time, day and night.
III. Plants photosynthesise only in light.
IV. In bright light, a plant gives out more oxygen than it uses.
Which are correct?
explanation: Every living cell respires continuously (II true, I false). Photosynthesis needs light (III). In bright light the rate of photosynthesis exceeds respiration, so there is a net release of oxygen (IV). At night only respiration occurs, so plants release CO₂.
misconception: The idea that plants respire only at night is a common misconception.
hints: Do plant cells need energy during the day?

subject: Biology
q: Many endurance athletes train for several weeks at high altitude, where the air contains less oxygen per breath. What benefit do they gain when they return to sea level?
options: Their bodies have made more red blood cells and haemoglobin, so their blood carries more oxygen.
Their hearts beat more slowly forever.
explanation: Low oxygen at altitude triggers the kidneys to release the hormone erythropoietin (EPO), which stimulates red blood cell production. Back at sea level, the extra red cells and haemoglobin deliver more oxygen to the muscles, improving endurance for a while.
hints: What carries oxygen in the blood?
How might the body respond to less oxygen over several weeks?

subject: Biology
q: Which word equation summarises aerobic respiration?
options: Glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy
explanation: Aerobic respiration oxidises glucose completely using oxygen: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + energy. The second equation is photosynthesis; the last two are anaerobic respiration in muscle and yeast.
misconception: Photosynthesis is roughly the reverse of aerobic respiration.
hints: Aerobic means “with oxygen”.

subject: Biology
q: How do insects such as grasshoppers get oxygen to their body cells?
options: Through tiny openings called spiracles that lead into a network of air tubes (tracheae)
explanation: Insects have spiracles along the sides of the body. Air passes along branching tracheae directly to the tissues; their blood plays little part in carrying oxygen. This system limits how large insects can grow.
hints: Look for small holes along an insect’s abdomen.

subject: Biology
q: During hard exercise, breathing becomes faster and deeper. What is the main signal the brain responds to?
options: A rise in carbon dioxide (and acidity) in the blood
A fall in nitrogen in the blood
explanation: Working muscles respire faster and produce more CO₂, which makes the blood slightly more acidic. Chemoreceptors detect this, and the respiratory centre in the medulla increases the rate and depth of breathing — removing CO₂ and bringing in more O₂.
misconception: The main trigger is excess CO₂, not lack of O₂.
hints: Which waste gas builds up when muscles work hard?

subject: Biology
q: How many chambers does the human heart have?
options: Two — one atrium and one ventricle
Four — two atria and two ventricles
Three — two atria and one ventricle
explanation: The human heart has two upper atria that receive blood and two lower, more muscular ventricles that pump it out. Fish have two chambers; amphibians and most reptiles have three.
hints: Atria receive; ventricles pump.

subject: Biology
q: Humans have a “double circulation”, in which blood passes through the heart twice in each complete circuit. What is the main advantage?
options: It makes the heart beat twice as fast.
It lets blood skip the lungs.
It doubles the amount of blood.
Oxygenated and deoxygenated blood stay separate, and blood can be pumped to the body at high pressure after returning from the lungs.
explanation: One circuit (pulmonary) sends blood to the lungs at low pressure; the other (systemic) sends oxygen-rich blood to the body at high pressure. Keeping them separate delivers fully oxygenated blood efficiently — important for warm-blooded animals with high energy needs.
hints: What would happen if blood went straight from the lungs to the body without returning to the heart?

subject: Biology
q: What is the function of the valves in the heart and in veins?
explanation: Valves are flaps that open in one direction only. Heart valves stop blood flowing back into the atria or ventricles when they contract; vein valves stop blood pooling as it travels back to the heart at low pressure, especially from the legs.
hints: Think of a one-way door.

subject: Biology
q: A heart beats at an average of 72 beats per minute. About how many times does it beat in one day?
explanation: 72 × 60 × 24 = 103,680 ≈ 1.04 × 10⁵ beats per day — about 38 million beats a year.
misconception: 4320 is the number of beats per hour.
hints: Beats per minute × minutes per hour × hours per day.

subject: Biology
q: Why do arteries have thick, muscular, elastic walls, while veins have thinner walls and valves?
options: Arteries carry blood at high pressure from the heart; veins carry blood at low pressure back to the heart.
Veins are closer to the heart.
explanation: Each heartbeat pushes blood into the arteries at high pressure; their thick elastic walls withstand it and smooth out the flow. By the time blood reaches the veins its pressure is low, so thin walls suffice, but valves are needed to keep it moving towards the heart.
hints: Where is blood pressure highest?

subject: Biology
q: In which blood vessels does the exchange of oxygen, nutrients and wastes with body cells take place?
explanation: Capillaries are microscopic vessels with walls only one cell thick, running close to every cell. Substances diffuse across their walls. Arteries and veins have walls too thick for exchange.
hints: Which vessels are only one cell thick?

subject: Biology
q: A normal adult blood pressure reading is often given as 120/80 mmHg. What do the two numbers represent?
options: Pressure when the ventricles contract (systolic) and when they relax (diastolic)
Pressure in arteries and in veins
explanation: The higher (systolic) value is the arterial pressure as the ventricles contract; the lower (diastolic) value is the pressure while the heart relaxes between beats. It is measured with a sphygmomanometer.
hints: The heart alternately contracts and relaxes.

subject: Biology
q: Which is a function of lymph?
options: Carrying absorbed fats from the intestine and returning leaked tissue fluid to the blood
explanation: Lymph is the fluid that leaks out of capillaries into tissues and is collected by lymph vessels. Lacteals in the villi absorb digested fats into the lymph. Lymph nodes along the vessels contain white cells that filter out microbes.
hints: Fats are absorbed into the lacteals of the villi.

subject: Biology
q: Mature human red blood cells have no nucleus. What advantage does this give?
options: More space for haemoglobin, so each cell can carry more oxygen
They can make their own proteins.
explanation: Losing the nucleus (and mitochondria) leaves the cell packed with haemoglobin and gives it a flexible biconcave shape with a large surface area for gas exchange. The cost is a short life of about 120 days, as the cell cannot repair itself.
hints: What fills the inside of a red blood cell?

subject: Biology
q: How do white blood cells protect the body?
options: Some engulf microbes (phagocytosis) and others produce antibodies
They carry oxygen to the immune system
explanation: Phagocytes surround and digest bacteria; lymphocytes produce antibodies that attack specific pathogens and form memory cells. Platelets, not white cells, help with clotting.
hints: Two main types: one engulfs, one makes antibodies.

subject: Biology
q: A fish has a two-chambered heart, and its blood passes through the heart only once per circuit (heart → gills → body → heart). What is a consequence of this single circulation?
options: Blood loses much of its pressure in the gill capillaries, so it flows to the body at low pressure.
Fish blood moves faster than human blood.
explanation: In a single circulation, blood pumped through the fine capillaries of the gills loses most of its pressure before reaching the body. This is enough for cold-blooded fish supported by water, but would be too slow to supply the high oxygen demand of a warm-blooded animal — one reason mammals and birds evolved double circulation.
hints: What happens to blood pressure when blood is forced through narrow capillaries?
Is there a second pump after the gills?

subject: Biology
q: Plants have no heart, yet water rises over 100 m to the top of the tallest trees. What mainly pulls it up?
options: Transpiration from the leaves, creating a tension that pulls a continuous column of water up the xylem
Root pressure alone pushing the water up
explanation: Water evaporating from leaf cells and leaving through stomata (transpiration) pulls on the water in the xylem. Water molecules stick to each other (cohesion) and to the xylem walls (adhesion), so the whole column is drawn up from the roots. Root pressure helps a little in small plants.
misconception: Root pressure can push water only a few metres; it cannot explain tall trees.
hints: What happens to water at the leaves?
Water molecules attract each other strongly.

subject: Biology
q: How does an Amoeba usually reproduce?
explanation: Amoeba divides its nucleus and then its cytoplasm, forming two identical daughter cells — binary fission. It is a quick, asexual method common among unicellular organisms.
hints: “Binary” means two.

subject: Biology
q: In Hydra and yeast, a small outgrowth develops on the parent, grows and eventually detaches as a new individual. What is this method called?
explanation: In budding, a bud forms through repeated cell division at one place on the parent and grows into a new organism, which may separate. It is a form of asexual reproduction producing genetically identical offspring.
hints: The new organism grows from a small outgrowth.

subject: Biology
q: A slice of moist bread left in a warm place develops fuzzy grey-black growth after a few days. How did the bread mould (Rhizopus) reach it?
options: Through tiny spores carried in the air, which germinate on moist food
It formed spontaneously from the bread
By budding from yeast in the bread
explanation: Rhizopus produces huge numbers of microscopic spores in sporangia (the black dots). Spores float in the air and grow into new hyphae wherever they land on moist food. Living things arise only from other living things, not spontaneously.
misconception: Mould does not arise spontaneously — Pasteur’s experiments disproved that idea.
hints: What are the black dots on the mould?

subject: Biology
q: If a flatworm (Planaria) is cut into several pieces, each piece can grow into a complete worm. This ability is called:
explanation: Planaria contain many undifferentiated cells that can divide and specialise to rebuild the missing parts. Regeneration differs from ordinary reproduction because it usually follows injury rather than being the normal way of producing offspring.
hints: The worm re-grows lost parts.

subject: Biology
q: Asexual reproduction is faster and needs only one parent. Why, then, do most plants and animals reproduce sexually?
options: Asexual reproduction cannot happen in multicellular organisms.
Sexual reproduction mixes genes from two parents, producing variation that helps a population survive changes and diseases.
explanation: Meiosis and fertilisation shuffle and combine genes, so offspring differ from their parents and each other. In a changing environment or when a new disease appears, some individuals are likely to survive. Variation is also the raw material for evolution.
misconception: Many multicellular organisms (plants, Hydra, Planaria) do reproduce asexually.
hints: How do offspring of sexual reproduction compare with each other?
Why might variation help when the environment changes?

subject: Biology
q: Which parts of a flower make up the stamen (the male part)?
explanation: The stamen has a filament (stalk) topped by an anther, where pollen grains (containing male gametes) are made. The pistil (carpel) — stigma, style and ovary — is the female part.
hints: Pollen is made in the …?

subject: Biology
q: What is the difference between self-pollination and cross-pollination?
options: Self: pollen reaches the stigma of the same flower or plant; cross: pollen comes from another plant of the same species.
Self: done by insects; cross: done by wind.
Self: happens after fertilisation; cross: before.
explanation: Cross-pollination, carried by wind, water, insects or birds, mixes genes from two plants and increases variation. Many plants have adaptations (separate male and female flowers, different maturity times) to encourage it.
misconception: The agent (wind, insect) does not define self- or cross-pollination; the source of pollen does.
hints: Where does the pollen come from in each case?

subject: Biology
q: Cultivated bananas are seedless. How are new banana plants produced, and what is one risk of this method?
options: By pollination by bats; plants become too varied.
By grafting onto mango trees; fruits become sour.
From seeds hidden in the peel; there is no risk.
By vegetative propagation from suckers or tissue culture; all plants are genetically identical and equally vulnerable to the same disease.
explanation: Without seeds, bananas are grown from suckers (shoots from the underground stem) or tissue culture, so they are clones. The Gros Michel variety was largely wiped out by Panama disease in the 20th century, and today’s Cavendish faces similar threats.
hints: Without seeds, which kind of reproduction is left?
What does cloning do to genetic variation?

subject: Biology
q: In human reproduction, where does fertilisation of the egg usually take place?
explanation: An egg released from the ovary travels along the oviduct, where it may meet sperm and be fertilised. The zygote divides as it moves to the uterus, where it implants in the thickened uterine lining.
misconception: The embryo implants and develops in the uterus, but fertilisation happens earlier, in the oviduct.
hints: The egg is fertilised on its journey from the ovary.

subject: Biology
q: What is the main role of the placenta during pregnancy?
options: To carry sperm to the egg
To pump blood for the foetus
To exchange nutrients, oxygen and wastes between the mother’s blood and the foetus’s blood without the two bloods mixing
explanation: The placenta has a huge surface of villi close to the mother’s blood. Glucose, amino acids and oxygen diffuse to the foetus; CO₂ and urea pass back. It also produces hormones that maintain pregnancy. Harmful substances like alcohol and nicotine can also cross it.
hints: How does the foetus get oxygen and food?

subject: Biology
q: Why does menstruation occur roughly once a month in women of reproductive age?
options: The uterus shrinks permanently each month.
The ovaries release blood every month.
Menstruation is caused by an infection.
If the egg is not fertilised, the thickened lining of the uterus breaks down and is shed with blood.
explanation: Each cycle the uterus lining thickens with blood vessels to receive a fertilised egg. If fertilisation does not occur, hormone levels fall and the lining breaks down, leaving the body as menstrual flow. The cycle is controlled by hormones such as oestrogen and progesterone.
hints: Why does the uterus lining thicken in the first place?

subject: Biology
q: Before a cell divides, its DNA is copied. The copying is extremely accurate but not perfect. Why is this slight inaccuracy important in biology?
options: Occasional copying errors (mutations) create variation, the raw material on which natural selection acts.
It prevents any change in species over time.
It allows cells to make more energy.
explanation: Mutations are mostly harmless or harmful, but a few produce useful traits. Over many generations, natural selection favours individuals with helpful variations, so species change. Perfectly accurate copying would leave no variation to select from.
hints: What would happen to evolution if every copy were perfect?

subject: Biology
q: Gregor Mendel discovered the basic laws of inheritance through experiments on which organism?
explanation: In the 1850s–60s Mendel crossed thousands of pea plants with clearly contrasting traits (tall/dwarf, round/wrinkled seeds). Peas were ideal: easy to grow, quick generations and controllable pollination. Fruit flies were used later by T. H. Morgan.
hints: He worked in a monastery garden.

subject: Biology
q: A pure-breeding tall pea plant (TT) is crossed with a pure-breeding dwarf plant (tt). All the offspring (F1) are tall. What is their genotype?
options: A mixture of TT and tt
explanation: Each offspring receives one T from the tall parent and one t from the dwarf parent, so all are Tt. They look tall because T is dominant; the recessive t is hidden but still present, and dwarf plants reappear when F1 plants are crossed together.
hints: What can each parent pass on?

subject: Biology
q: A normal human body cell has 46 chromosomes. How are they organised?
options: 23 pairs: 22 pairs of autosomes and 1 pair of sex chromosomes
22 pairs of sex chromosomes and 1 pair of autosomes
explanation: Each pair has one chromosome from the mother and one from the father. Pairs 1–22 are autosomes; the 23rd pair is the sex chromosomes (XX in females, XY in males).
hints: How many pairs make 46?

subject: Biology
q: A couple’s first two children are both boys. What is the probability that their third child will be a girl?
explanation: Each pregnancy is an independent event: the father’s sperm carries X or Y with equal probability, regardless of previous children. So the chance of a girl is still 1/2. (1/8 would be the probability, before any child is born, that all three are boys.)
misconception: Earlier outcomes do not change the probability of the next — this is the “gambler’s fallacy”.
hints: Does the sex of earlier children affect which sperm fertilises the next egg?
Is each birth independent?

subject: Biology
q: When does a recessive trait appear in the phenotype of an individual?
options: Only when the individual has two copies of the recessive allele
Whenever one copy of the recessive allele is present
explanation: A dominant allele masks a recessive one. The recessive trait shows only in homozygous recessive individuals (e.g. tt). Heterozygotes (Tt) are carriers: they show the dominant trait but can pass on the recessive allele.
hints: What does a dominant allele do to a recessive one?

subject: Biology
q: Free earlobes (E) are dominant over attached earlobes (e). Two parents with free earlobes have a child with attached earlobes. What are the parents’ genotypes?
options: One is EE and one is Ee
explanation: The child with attached earlobes must be ee, receiving one e from each parent. Both parents show free earlobes, so each must also carry an E: both are Ee. Each further child has a 1/4 chance of attached earlobes.
misconception: If either parent were EE, every child would receive at least one E.
hints: What genotype must the child have?
Where did each of the child’s alleles come from?

subject: Biology
q: Who proposed the double-helix structure of DNA in 1953, using X-ray diffraction images produced in Rosalind Franklin’s laboratory?
options: Har Gobind Khorana and Marshall Nirenberg
explanation: Watson and Crick built their double-helix model in 1953, relying on X-ray photographs (notably “Photo 51”) from Rosalind Franklin and Raymond Gosling and data from Maurice Wilkins. Khorana and Nirenberg later helped crack the genetic code (Nobel Prize 1968).
hints: The model was announced in 1953 at Cambridge.

subject: Biology
q: What is a mutation?
options: An organism moving to a new habitat
A change in the sequence of DNA
explanation: A mutation is a change in the DNA base sequence of a gene or chromosome. It can occur by copying errors or be caused by radiation and some chemicals. Mutations in gametes can be inherited.
hints: It happens in the genetic material.

subject: Biology
q: In peas, round seeds (R) are dominant over wrinkled (r) and yellow (Y) over green (y). Two plants heterozygous for both traits (RrYy × RrYy) produce 160 seeds. About how many are expected to be round and yellow?
explanation: The dihybrid cross gives round-yellow : round-green : wrinkled-yellow : wrinkled-green = 9 : 3 : 3 : 1. Round and yellow = 9/16 × 160 = 90. (Each 3/16 class gives 30; the 1/16 class gives 10.)
misconception: 30 is the number for one of the 3/16 classes.
hints: Recall the 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 ratio.
Which class shows both dominant traits?

subject: Biology
q: Why do identical twins have the same genes?
options: They develop from a single fertilised egg that splits into two embryos.
They develop from two eggs fertilised by two sperm.
They share the same placenta only.
They are born on the same day.
explanation: Identical (monozygotic) twins come from one zygote that splits early in development, so their DNA is the same. Non-identical (fraternal) twins come from two different eggs and two sperm and are no more alike genetically than other siblings.
hints: How many zygotes are involved?

subject: Biology
q: Charles Darwin’s observations of finches with differently shaped beaks on the Galápagos Islands supported which idea?
explanation: Darwin noticed that finches on different islands had beaks suited to different foods (seeds, insects, cactus). He proposed that individuals better suited to their environment survive and reproduce more, so populations change over time — natural selection (On the Origin of Species, 1859).
hints: Different beaks suited different foods.

subject: Biology
q: In undisturbed layers of sedimentary rock, fossils in the deeper layers are generally older than those near the surface. Why?
options: Sediment is deposited layer upon layer over time, so lower layers formed first.
Deeper layers are warmer and preserve fossils better.
explanation: Sediments settle in sequence, with newer layers on top of older ones (the principle of superposition). This gives the relative age of fossils; radioactive dating of rocks gives their absolute age. The sequence shows simpler life forms in older layers.
hints: Which layer was laid down first?

subject: Biology
q: The wings of a butterfly and the wings of a bird both allow flight but have completely different structures and origins. They are examples of:
explanation: Analogous organs perform similar functions but evolved independently, with different structures (insect wings are thin cuticle; bird wings are modified forelimbs with bones and feathers). They show convergent evolution, not common ancestry.
misconception: Homologous organs share structure and origin; analogous organs share only function.
hints: Similar job, different build.

subject: Biology
q: Lamarck suggested that giraffes got long necks because each generation stretched to reach high leaves and passed the stretched necks to their offspring. Why is this explanation rejected?
options: Neck length is not affected by genes.
Characteristics acquired during an animal’s lifetime do not change the DNA in its gametes, so they are not inherited.
explanation: Stretching, exercise or injury changes body cells, not the genes passed on through eggs and sperm. Darwin’s explanation fits the evidence: giraffes varied in neck length; those with slightly longer necks fed better in droughts, survived and reproduced more, so the trait spread.
misconception: A bodybuilder’s children are not born with bigger muscles.
hints: Do changes to body cells reach the gametes?
How would natural selection explain long necks?

subject: Biology
q: The human appendix and wisdom teeth have little or no function today. What are such structures called, and what do they suggest?
options: Vestigial organs — evidence that our ancestors used them
Analogous organs — evidence of convergent evolution
explanation: Vestigial organs are reduced remnants of structures that were functional in ancestors. The appendix is linked to the larger caecum of plant-eating mammals; wisdom teeth to ancestors with larger jaws for tougher food. (The appendix may still have a minor role in immunity.)
hints: “Vestige” means a trace of something that once existed.

subject: Biology
q: A population of lizards is split when a section of land becomes an island. After thousands of generations, the island lizards can no longer breed with the mainland lizards. What process has occurred?
options: Speciation through geographical isolation and different natural selection
explanation: Separated populations no longer exchange genes. Different mutations arise and different environments favour different traits, so the populations drift apart genetically. Eventually they can no longer interbreed — they have become separate species.
hints: What stops genes flowing between the two groups?
What makes them change differently?

subject: Biology
q: Cabbage, cauliflower, broccoli and kale were all bred from the same wild mustard plant. What process produced such different vegetables?
options: Artificial selection — humans chose and bred plants with the features they wanted
explanation: Over centuries, farmers repeatedly bred plants with larger leaves (kale, cabbage), larger flower clusters (broccoli, cauliflower) or swollen stems (kohlrabi). This artificial selection shows how strongly selection can change a species — Darwin used it as an analogy.
hints: Who chose which plants to breed?

subject: Biology
q: Fossils of Archaeopteryx show feathers and wings like a bird, but also teeth, clawed fingers and a long bony tail like a reptile. Why is it important for the study of evolution?
options: It is a living bird found today.
It proves birds came before reptiles.
It shows that feathers evolved in fish.
It is a transitional form, supporting the idea that birds evolved from reptile-like ancestors (dinosaurs).
explanation: Archaeopteryx (about 150 million years old) combines features of two groups, as evolution predicts for intermediate forms. Many more feathered dinosaur fossils have since been found, strongly supporting the dinosaur origin of birds.
hints: It has features of which two groups?

subject: Biology
q: In a pond ecosystem, which organisms are the main producers?
explanation: Producers make their own food by photosynthesis and form the base of the food chain. In ponds, these are microscopic phytoplankton, larger algae and water plants. Fish and frogs are consumers; bacteria and fungi are decomposers.
hints: Which organisms photosynthesise?

subject: Biology
q: Why is a food web more stable than a single food chain?
options: Consumers have several food sources, so the loss of one species does not necessarily collapse the system.
explanation: In a food web, many chains interconnect. If one prey species declines, predators can switch to another, and populations adjust. In a single chain, removing one link starves everything above it.
hints: What happens to a predator in a single chain if its only prey disappears?

subject: Biology
q: In a single large banyan tree supporting thousands of insects, which in turn feed hundreds of birds, the pyramid of NUMBERS is inverted at the base. Why?
options: One producer (the tree) is huge, supporting many smaller consumers, so producer numbers are fewer than primary consumers.
explanation: A pyramid of numbers counts individuals, not their size. A single tree can feed thousands of insects. The pyramid of ENERGY, however, is never inverted: energy always decreases at each level.
misconception: Only the number of individuals is inverted; energy still decreases upward.
hints: Is the pyramid counting individuals or energy?

subject: Biology
q: In the food chain plants → caterpillars → small birds → hawk, the hawk receives 50 kJ of energy. Using the 10% law, how much energy must the plants have captured?
explanation: Working backwards, each level must hold about 10 times the energy of the level above: small birds 500 kJ, caterpillars 5000 kJ, plants 50,000 kJ. Only about 0.1% of the plants’ energy reaches the hawk — why top predators are rare.
misconception: 5000 kJ stops one level short; there are three transfers.
hints: Each level down needs about 10 times more energy.
Count the transfers from plants to hawk.

subject: Biology
q: Which process REMOVES carbon dioxide from the atmosphere in the carbon cycle?
explanation: Plants, algae and some bacteria take in CO₂ and turn it into sugars by photosynthesis. Respiration, combustion and decomposition all return CO₂ to the air. Oceans also dissolve large amounts of CO₂.
hints: Which process uses CO₂ as a raw material?

subject: Biology
q: In the nitrogen cycle, which bacteria convert nitrates in the soil back into nitrogen gas?
explanation: Denitrifying bacteria, mostly in waterlogged, oxygen-poor soils, break down nitrates and release N₂ to the atmosphere, completing the cycle. Nitrogen-fixing bacteria do the opposite; nitrifying bacteria convert ammonia to nitrites and nitrates.
hints: “De-nitrify” means removing nitrogen compounds from soil.

subject: Biology
q: Besides bacteria, which natural physical event fixes some atmospheric nitrogen into compounds plants can use?
explanation: The enormous energy of a lightning flash splits N₂ and O₂ molecules, forming nitrogen oxides. These dissolve in rain to form dilute nitric acid, which reaches the soil as nitrates. Industrially, the Haber process fixes nitrogen to make fertiliser.
hints: N₂ has a very strong triple bond — what can break it?

subject: Biology
q: Apart from evaporation from oceans and lakes, what is the major way in which water from land returns to the atmosphere?
explanation: Plants draw water from the soil and lose most of it as vapour through their leaves. Large forests release so much water vapour that they influence rainfall — removing forests can make a region drier.
hints: Plants lose water through their stomata.

subject: Biology
q: Frogs in a rice field are collected in large numbers for sale. What changes would you most expect in the field over the next few seasons?
options: No change, because frogs do not eat insects.
Rice plants grow faster because frogs compete with them.
Insect pests decrease and snakes increase.
Insect pests increase and crop damage rises, while snakes that eat frogs decline.
explanation: Frogs eat many insect pests. Removing them releases the insects from predation, so pest numbers and crop damage rise, often leading to more pesticide use. Snakes and birds that depend on frogs lose a food source. Indian frog exports were restricted partly for this reason.
hints: What do frogs eat?
What eats frogs?

subject: Biology
q: A lichen is formed by a fungus and an alga living closely together. The fungus provides shelter and absorbs water; the alga makes food. What type of relationship is this?
explanation: In mutualism both organisms gain. Lichens can live on bare rock where neither partner could survive alone, and they help start soil formation. Root nodules (legume + Rhizobium) are another example.
hints: Does each partner gain something?

subject: Biology
q: Cuscuta (amarbel), a yellow leafless plant, twines around other plants and draws food from them through special roots. It is an example of:
explanation: Cuscuta has no chlorophyll. It inserts haustoria (sucking roots) into the host’s phloem and takes its nutrients, harming the host — parasitism. It can seriously damage crops.
hints: It has no green colour — how does it feed?

subject: Biology
q: The table shows estimated numbers of hares and lynx (a predator of hares) in a forest. Which statement is best supported?
options: Lynx cause hare numbers to rise.
Lynx numbers rise after hare numbers rise and fall after hares decline, so predator numbers lag behind prey numbers.
explanation: Hares peak in year 3; lynx peak in year 4. More food lets predators breed more, but then predation (and food shortage) cuts hare numbers, after which lynx decline. Predator–prey cycles with a time lag are a classic ecological pattern.
hints: In which year does each population peak?
Which peaks first?

subject: Biology
q: Which of these is an ABIOTIC component of an ecosystem?
explanation: Abiotic factors are non-living: sunlight, temperature, water, soil minerals, air. Biotic factors are living organisms — producers, consumers and decomposers.
hints: “A-biotic” means not living.

subject: Biology
q: Why do most leaves look green?
options: Chlorophyll absorbs mainly red and blue light and reflects green light.
Green light is the brightest part of sunlight.
explanation: Chlorophyll absorbs strongly in the blue and red parts of the spectrum and uses that energy for photosynthesis. Green light is mostly reflected or transmitted, so leaves appear green.
misconception: The colour we see is the light that is NOT absorbed.
hints: Is the colour we see absorbed or reflected?

subject: Biology
q: A variegated leaf (with green and white patches) from a plant kept in sunlight is tested with iodine. Only the parts that were green turn blue-black. What does this show?
options: Iodine reacts only with green cells.
Light is not needed for photosynthesis.
Chlorophyll is needed for photosynthesis (starch formation).
explanation: Both green and white parts received the same light, carbon dioxide and water; only the green parts contain chlorophyll. Starch formed only there, so chlorophyll is necessary. (The plant is first destarched so that any starch found was made during the experiment.)
hints: What is the only difference between green and white parts?

subject: Biology
q: A destarched plant has one leaf enclosed in a sealed bag containing potassium hydroxide (which absorbs CO₂). After a day in sunlight, this leaf gives a negative starch test while other leaves are positive. What does this show?
options: Carbon dioxide is needed for photosynthesis.
explanation: The bagged leaf had light, water and chlorophyll but no CO₂, and made no starch. Other leaves with normal air did. So CO₂ is a necessary raw material for photosynthesis.
hints: What did the potassium hydroxide remove?

subject: Biology
q: A greenhouse grower raises the CO₂ concentration inside from 0.04% to 0.1%. The tomato plants grow faster at first, but raising CO₂ further has no extra effect. Why?
options: Plants cannot use more than 0.1% CO₂ because it is poisonous.
CO₂ stops working after one day.
At first CO₂ was the limiting factor; once it is plentiful, another factor such as light or temperature limits the rate.
explanation: The rate of photosynthesis is limited by whichever factor is in shortest supply. Adding CO₂ helps until another factor — light intensity, temperature or chlorophyll — becomes limiting. Growers often raise light and temperature together with CO₂.
hints: Can a rate be limited by more than one factor at once?
What else does photosynthesis need?

subject: Biology
q: Root hairs are long, thin outgrowths of root epidermal cells. How do they help the plant?
options: They greatly increase the surface area for absorbing water and minerals from the soil.
They anchor the plant by gripping stones.
explanation: Millions of root hairs reach between soil particles and multiply the absorbing surface many times. Water enters by osmosis and minerals by diffusion and active transport. They are delicate, which is why transplanted seedlings often wilt.
hints: What does a larger surface area allow?

subject: Biology
q: A potted seedling is laid on its side in the dark. After a few days, its root curves downward and its shoot curves upward. What do these responses show?
options: Roots are positively geotropic and shoots negatively geotropic.
explanation: Geotropism (gravitropism) is growth in response to gravity. In the dark, light cannot be the cause. Roots grow towards gravity (into the soil, finding water and anchorage); shoots grow away from it (towards where light usually is). Auxin redistribution causes the bending.
hints: The plant was in the dark — so what stimulus remains?

subject: Biology
q: When touched, the leaflets of Mimosa pudica (touch-me-not) fold within seconds. How does this movement differ from a shoot bending towards light?
options: It is caused by muscles in the leaf.
It is caused by faster growth on one side.
It is controlled by a nervous system.
It is caused by a rapid loss of water (turgor) from special cells, not by growth.
explanation: Phototropism is a slow growth response driven by auxin. Mimosa’s folding is a fast nastic movement: touch triggers cells at the base of each leaflet (the pulvinus) to lose water, so they go limp and the leaflets fold. Plants have no nerves or muscles, though electrical signals pass along cells.
misconception: Plants have no nervous system or muscles.
hints: Can growth happen in a few seconds?
What makes plant cells firm or limp?

subject: Biology
q: In a bean seed, what is the role of the two large cotyledons?
options: They protect the seed from water.
They are the flower of the plant.
They store food for the growing seedling until it can photosynthesise.
explanation: Cotyledons (seed leaves) store starch, protein and oil, which are broken down and used for energy and growth during germination. In some seeds they come above ground and turn green briefly.
hints: What does a seedling use before its leaves grow?

subject: Biology
q: Bubbles are seen rising from a cut stem of the water plant Hydrilla placed in sunlight. When the plant is moved into a dim corner, fewer bubbles appear. What are the bubbles, and what does the change show?
options: Mainly oxygen from photosynthesis; the rate of photosynthesis depends on light intensity.
Water vapour; plants sweat in light.
Nitrogen; plants fix nitrogen in light.
Carbon dioxide from respiration; respiration needs light.
explanation: Photosynthesis releases oxygen, which escapes as bubbles. Counting bubbles per minute is a simple way to compare rates: in dimmer light, photosynthesis slows and fewer bubbles form.
hints: Which gas does photosynthesis release?

subject: Biology
q: A lamp 10 cm from a Hydrilla plant produces 40 bubbles per minute. Light intensity falls with the square of the distance. If light is the only limiting factor and bubble rate is proportional to light intensity, how many bubbles per minute would you predict with the lamp at 20 cm?
explanation: Doubling the distance reduces light intensity to (1/2)² = 1/4. If the rate is proportional to intensity, 40 × 1/4 = 10 bubbles per minute. Real results often differ a little because other factors start to limit or because the lamp also heats the water.
misconception: 20 assumes intensity falls in proportion to distance, not distance squared.
hints: Intensity ∝ 1/d². What is the intensity at twice the distance?
Rate ∝ intensity.

subject: Biology
q: Unlike water in the xylem, which only moves upward, food in the phloem can move both up and down the plant. Why is this useful?
options: It lets the plant lose sugar faster.
Sugar can be sent from leaves to wherever it is needed — down to roots and storage organs or up to growing buds and fruits.
explanation: This transport of food (translocation) moves sugars from “sources” (mature leaves, storage organs in spring) to “sinks” (roots, tubers, buds, fruits). Its direction changes with the season and the plant’s needs.
hints: Where is food made, and where is it needed?

subject: Biology
q: Fruit sellers sometimes keep unripe bananas with a ripe one in a closed box to speed up ripening. Which plant hormone, given off by the ripe fruit, is responsible?
explanation: Ethylene is a gaseous plant hormone that triggers ripening. Ripe fruit releases it, and in an enclosed space it hastens ripening of nearby fruit. Auxin controls growth towards light; gibberellins promote stem elongation and seed germination.
hints: This hormone is a gas.

subject: Biology
q: Pitcher plants and sundews trap and digest insects, even though they are green and photosynthesise. Why do they do this?
options: They grow in nutrient-poor (especially nitrogen-poor) soils and get extra nitrogen and minerals from the insects.
They need insects for energy because they have no chlorophyll.
They use insects to pollinate the trap.
explanation: Insectivorous plants live in bogs and wet places where soil lacks nitrogen. They still make their own sugars by photosynthesis, but digesting insects supplies nitrogen (for proteins) and other minerals.
misconception: They do photosynthesise; the insects supply nutrients, not mainly energy.
hints: Which essential element is often scarce in boggy soils?

subject: Biology
q: Which part of the brain controls involuntary actions such as heartbeat, breathing and swallowing?
explanation: The medulla, in the hindbrain connecting to the spinal cord, regulates vital involuntary functions. Damage to it is life-threatening.
hints: It joins the brain to the spinal cord.

subject: Biology
q: A person with an underactive thyroid gland may feel tired, gain weight and feel cold. Which hormone is deficient?
explanation: Thyroxine regulates metabolic rate — how fast cells use energy. Too little slows metabolism, causing fatigue, weight gain and cold intolerance. Its production requires iodine.
hints: Which gland is in the neck?

subject: Biology
q: After a sugary meal, blood glucose rises and the pancreas releases insulin. Several hours later, when glucose falls, it releases glucagon. What principle does this illustrate?
options: Positive feedback — the change is amplified
Negative feedback — a change triggers a response that reverses it, keeping blood glucose steady
Digestion of glucose by the pancreas
Reflex action through the spinal cord
explanation: Insulin makes cells take up glucose and the liver store it as glycogen, lowering blood glucose. Glucagon makes the liver break down glycogen, raising it. Opposing hormones correct changes in either direction — homeostasis by negative feedback. Body temperature and water balance are controlled similarly.
hints: Do insulin and glucagon push glucose the same way?
What does each response do to the original change?

subject: Biology
q: On a hot day your skin looks flushed and you sweat. How do these responses cool the body?
options: Blood vessels close to keep heat in.
Sweat is colder than the body.
Blood vessels near the skin widen so more heat is lost from the blood, and evaporating sweat removes latent heat.
explanation: Vasodilation brings more warm blood close to the surface, where heat is lost by radiation and convection. Sweat glands release water that evaporates, taking latent heat from the skin. In cold weather the opposite happens: vessels narrow and shivering generates heat.
hints: Why does evaporation cool a surface?

subject: Biology
q: After a long, hot game with little to drink, a player passes only a small amount of dark yellow urine. What is happening in the body?
options: The brain releases more antidiuretic hormone (ADH), so the kidneys reabsorb more water and produce concentrated urine.
The player has drunk too much water.
The bladder is storing urine for later.
explanation: Water loss by sweating raises the concentration of the blood. The pituitary gland releases ADH, which makes the kidney tubules more permeable, so more water is reabsorbed into the blood. Urine becomes smaller in volume and more concentrated. Drinking water reverses this.
hints: The body has lost water — what should the kidneys do?
Which hormone controls water reabsorption?

subject: Biology
q: Tuberculosis (TB) is caused by which kind of microbe, and how does it usually spread?
options: A bacterium, spread through the air by coughing and sneezing
A fungus, spread by touching skin
A protozoan, spread by contaminated food
explanation: TB is caused by the bacterium Mycobacterium tuberculosis, mainly affecting the lungs. It spreads in droplets when infected people cough. It is curable with a long course of antibiotics; the BCG vaccine gives some protection.
hints: It is treated with antibiotics.

subject: Biology
q: How does a gene usually control a characteristic such as flower colour?
options: It is a type of carbohydrate.
It carries the instructions for making a particular protein, such as an enzyme that produces a pigment.
It changes the soil around the plant.
explanation: A gene’s DNA sequence codes for the order of amino acids in a protein. If the gene codes for a working enzyme in a pigment pathway, the flower is coloured; a mutant allele may make a non-working enzyme, giving white flowers.
hints: What molecules do genes code for?

subject: Biology
q: Red–green colour blindness is caused by a recessive allele on the X chromosome. Why is it much more common in men than in women?
options: Men have only one X chromosome, so a single recessive allele shows; women need two copies.
Women cannot inherit X chromosomes from their fathers.
The Y chromosome causes colour blindness.
explanation: Males are XY: whatever allele is on their single X is expressed, as the Y carries no matching gene. Females are XX: a normal allele on one X masks the recessive one, so they are usually carriers. About 8% of men but under 1% of women have red–green colour blindness.
hints: How many X chromosomes does a male have?
Is there a matching allele on the Y chromosome?

subject: Biology
q: Human height varies smoothly across a wide range, while ABO blood group falls into a few distinct categories. These are examples of:
explanation: Continuous variation (height, weight) shows a range of values, usually controlled by many genes plus the environment, and forms a bell-shaped graph. Discontinuous variation (blood group, tongue rolling) falls into clear categories and is usually controlled by one or a few genes.
hints: Can height take any value? Can blood group?

subject: Biology
q: Early embryos of fish, chickens and humans look remarkably similar, all with gill slit-like structures and tails. What does this suggest?
options: These vertebrates share a common ancestor.
Humans breathe with gills as adults.
explanation: Comparative embryology reveals shared developmental patterns inherited from a common ancestor. In humans, the pharyngeal (gill) arches develop into parts of the jaw, ear and throat rather than gills.
hints: Why would unrelated organisms share embryonic features?

subject: Biology
q: In 1953, Miller and Urey passed electric sparks through a sealed mixture of methane, ammonia, hydrogen and water vapour, imitating the early Earth. After a week, amino acids had formed. What did this suggest?
